paper_title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/

Code and data are available at https://github.com/gtcgh/SATE-Bench. 1 1. Introduction The visual perception of human behavior is fundamentally dynamic and multidimensional [16, 17, 20, 2933, 36, 40 42, 45, 46, 51, 55, 58, 59, 63, 6567]. In real environments such as collaborative sports [47] and operating rooms [38], severe mutual occlusion frequently obscures essential geometric cues, requiring an intelligent observer to actively seek alternative perspectives [2, 23, 53]. Despite the strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [1, 3, 4, 6, 50], current spatial evaluations remain primarily limited to passive observation. Standard Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmarks [10, 11, 18, 48, 56, 59, 60] provide predetermined set of images, thereby focusing on reasoning given that evidence while ignoring visual self-awareness [52], i.e., the capacity to recognize observational blind spots. When faced with heavily occluded views, such passive frameworks force models to rely on linguistic priors and hallucinate missing details rather than seeking new information. Existing interactive benchmarks [21, 53, 64] predominantly focus on synthetic environments and ego-centric trajectory planning, leaving real-world, human-centric exocentric exploration largely unexamined. This setting is inherently challenging: model must assess whether its current view is sufficient, decide which viewpoint to query next, and establish cross-view correspondence of people and objects across wide perspective shifts. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench. The acronym SATE reflects our core evaluation philosophy: to fully satisfy desire. An initial occluded view leaves the model hungry for information, compelling it to actively explore the spatial environment to sate its need for definitive visual evidence. We construct this benchmark by sampling 316 dense, realworld scenes from 10 diverse multi-view human-centric datasets, yielding 2,525 high-quality QA pairs with an average of 6.04 camera views per scene. To disentangle multi-view feature fusion from active ambiguity resolution, SATE-Bench pairs an Active exploration setting with Passive control. In the Active setting, the MLLM is initialized with single, severely occluded view and must autonomously judge whether it has sufficient evidence to answer; if not, it iteratively queries adjacent exocentric viewpoints (left or right) across multiple turns until the necessary spatial information is uncovered. Conversely, the Passive setting isolates pure multi-view spatial reasoning by providing comprehensive set of static views upfront, guaranteeing that the question is directly answerable without exploration. Comparing performance across both settings tests whether model knows when to seek new views and when it has gathered enough evidence to stop. SATE-Bench also incorporates an exponentially decaying reward to penalize redundant queries and quantify exploration efficiency. Benchmarking 12 state-of-the-art Table 1. Moreover, applying Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to Qwen2.5VL-3B shows that rewarding view-seeking boosts its active exploration rate from 0.2% to 72.8%, yet reduces accuracy from 30.4% to 17.9%, as the model moves more without learning when to stop or how to fuse the accumulated views. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: Novel Evaluation Protocol: We identify the limitations of passive evaluation and formulate diagnostic Active/Passive evaluation framework paired with an exponentially decaying efficiency reward to assess visual selfawareness and penalize redundant spatial queries. SATE-Bench: We curate an interactive benchmark of 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs for evaluating active exocentric view-exploration. Comprehensive Benchmarking: We evaluate state-ofthe-art MLLMs, showing through confidence probing and matched-view controls that premature stopping and insufficient evidence acquisition drive the ActivePassive gap. Active Exploration via GRPO: We show that GRPO boosts active view-seeking while uncovering trade-off between active exploration and reasoning accuracy. 2. Related Work 2.1. Multi-Image MLLM Benchmarks Recent multi-image MLLM benchmarks universally evaluate reasoning via static, passive observation [11, 13, 26, 34, 39, 48, 49, 5557, 61, 68]. Although recent multi-view evaluations like AllAnglesBench [59] and CVBench [19] explore cross-view correspondence and spatial perception, 2 Figure 2. Overview of the SATE-Bench Curation and Evaluation Pipeline. Our framework is constructed and deployed through four distinct stages. Steps 1 & 2 (Data Collection and Quality Control): We source dense, 360-degree multi-view captures across five cognitive spatial categories. Candidate question-answer pairs undergo rigorous human annotation and modification loop to guarantee accuracy, clarity, and appropriate difficulty. Step 3 (Active Exploration): The multi-turn interactive evaluation setting. The MLLM is initialized with single view and must dynamically query additional exocentric perspectives until it confidently resolves its visual uncertainty. Step 4 (Passive Observation): The single-turn control setting, where the model is provided static, comprehensive bag-offrames to yield direct prediction without the need for spatial view-exploration. they rely on pre-configured, static viewpoints. These benchmarks provide sparse perspective coverage (averaging just 3 views per scene in AllAnglesBench and 4 in CVBench) and fundamentally lack the interactive mechanics required to evaluate models active exploration abilities. When severe occlusion obscures important geometry, such passive frameworks force models to guess or hallucinate missing details rather than actively resolving visual ambiguity [7, 28]. While interactive setups like ActiView [53] permit 2D image cropping, they lack real-world 3D spatial complexity. Unlike prior benchmarks, as discussed in Table 1, that rely on passive multi-view aggregation, SATE-Bench requires active spatial reasoning by situating MLLMs within immersive 360-degree environments to plan exocentric viewpoints and resolve visual occlusions. 2.2. Active Visual Perception Active visual perception compels intelligent observers to dynamically adjust viewpoints to resolve uncertainty [2, 9, 52]. While recent benchmarks like Theory of Space [64] and ESI-Bench [21] advance active spatial reasoning, they focus predominantly on egocentric navigation within synthetic simulations to evaluate cognitive map construction and physical object manipulation. Similarly, ProactiveBench [8] assesses proactive querying behaviors but lacks complex multi-view spatial environments. In contrast, SATE-Bench targets active exocentric view-exploration in dense, real-world human-centric scenes. Rather than assessing embodied navigation or general proactivity, it isolates visual self-awareness under severe mutual occlusion, evaluating whether models can recognize observational blind spots and integrate cross-view geometry through step-penalized, Active/Passive diagnostic framework. 2.3. Multi-View Human-Centric Datasets Comprehending complex human behavior requires robust multi-view observations to overcome severe selfand mutual-occlusion. The community has developed diverse datasets capturing dense activities (M3GYM [54], Harmony4D [25], EgoHumans [24]), fine-grained interactions (HOI-M3 [62], Ego-Exo4D [15], core4D [35]), and occluded workflows (4D-OR [37], MM-OR [38]). While highly effective for advancing passive spatial tasks like 2D/3D pose estimation, human tracking, and human-object interaction detection, these datasets remain underutilized for interactive multi-turn conversational foundation model 3 evaluation. SATE-Bench reuses these static multi-view captures into dynamic exploratory arenas, challenging MLLMs to autonomously step through discrete spatial camera views to uncover obscured visual truths. 3. SATE-Bench 3.1. Benchmark Overview Humans inherently resolve spatial occlusions by actively exploring alternative viewpoints and internally fusing these multi-perspective observations. Yet, existing benchmarks [5, 8, 14, 19, 21, 22, 59, 64] primarily rely on single ego-centric views or passive, static image sets, leaving exocentric view-exploration and visual self-awareness largely unexamined. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATEBench. Rather than providing predetermined bag of frames, we situate the model within an interactive 360degree spatial environment. Initialized with single, heavily occluded view, the MLLM must explicitly recognize its visual uncertainty and dynamically query new exocentric perspectives to gather missing evidence. Through our decoupled framework of Active Exploration and Passive Observation, SATE-Bench evaluates whether an MLLM possesses the visual self-awareness to know what it cannot see, when to iteratively explore, and when to confidently answer. The overall framework is shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2. 3.2. Benchmark Curation Process 3.2.1. Task Definitions We define ten human-centric tasks across five cognitive dimensions to systematically evaluate spatial reasoning and view-exploration. Entity Counting (Human/Object) tests global spatial memory and cross-view re-identification, requiring models to resolve occlusions without doublecounting. Entity Existence (Human/Object) probes visual self-awareness and blind-spot recognition by challenging models to query new viewpoints to confirm target presence. Pose and Physical Interaction (Action & Pose / HumanObject Interaction) assesses granular geometric alignment and the resolution of severe self-occlusions. Global Relative Proximity (Distance to Human/Object) evaluates multi-view depth estimation and cross-perspective distance reasoning. Finally, View-Conditioned Spatial Geometry (Depth Ordering / Direction) tests perspective-taking, geometric projection, and dynamic coordinate frame alignment from specific, non-ego vantage points. 3.2.2. Data Collection real-world human-centric datasets, We source raw multi-view video sequences from diverse, including M3GYM [54], Harmony4D [25], HOI-M3 [62], EgoExo4D [15], EgoHumans [24], MvMHAT [12], Replay [44], 4D-OR [37], MM-OR [38], and core4D [35]. Benchmark Statistics The finalized SATE-Bench comprises 2,525 high-quality, multi-turn QA pairs spanning 10 human-centric tasks. Task distributions and text statistics are detailed in Tables 2 and 3. The detailed benchmark license, release plan, and more quantitative results are provided in the Appendix A. 3.4. Evaluation Metrics Accuracy: The exact-match percentage between the models final predicted option and the ground-truth answer, evaluated independently of the exploration trajectory. To ensure fair and robust evaluation, we initially apply rule-based parsing mechanism to extract the models final choice. If this fails due to irregular formatting, an LLMbased extractor is deployed as fallback mechanism. Exploration Efficiency Reward: To penalize redundant or excessively long spatial queries, we introduce an exponentially decaying reward metric. For given task category comprising questions, the reward is calculated as the average of the step-penalized scores across all questions. Single View Evaluation. In this setting, models are provided strictly with the initial view from the Active set and are evaluated passively (i.e., no spatial exploration is permitted). 4. Experiments and Main Results 4.1. Experimental Setup Baselines. To evaluate MLLM performance and disentangle exploration policies from downstream spatial reasoning, we provide 9 baselines in total. These include three foundational reference points (Random Guess, Blind Text-Only, and Human Baseline) alongside six evaluation settings applied to Gemini-3.1-flash-lite: Oracle-View, OracleTrajectory, Always Explore Left, Always Explore Right, Random-Walk, and Exhaustive-Search. By default, interaction histories are fully visible to models across all applicable evaluations, and the generation temperature is strictly set to 0.0 to guarantee deterministic and reproducible outputs. Detailed formulations for all 9 baselines and prompts are provided in the Appendix C. Evaluation Metrics. For the Passive setting (single-turn static observation), we report exact-match Average Accuracy (%) and total Inference Time (hours). For the Active setting (multi-turn spatial exploration), we provide more comprehensive assessment to capture interaction dynamics: 1) Average Accuracy (%), 2) Average Steps taken per query to reach final decision, 3) Average Reward (λ = 0.1), which penalizes redundant spatial queries to reflect view-seeking efficiency, 4) Active Rate (%), quantifying the frequency at which the model explicitly elects to shift its viewpoint rather than guessing directly from the initial occluded perspective, and 5) Inference Time (hours) for single process under the same hardware settings, while API models are subject to provider latency. 4.2. Main Results and Discussion Based on the comprehensive evaluation across the ten tasks in Table 4, we identify several insights regarding the active reasoning capabilities of MLLMs: Finding 1: The Passive-Active Performance Gap. There is severe degradation in accuracy when models transition from passive observation to active spatial exploration. For example, Gemini-3.5-flash achieves robust 69.2% accuracy when provided with sufficient static views, but drops to 56.8% in the Active setting. This discrepancy demonstrates that while MLLMs possess foundational multi-view fusion capabilities, they lack the visual self-awareness required to autonomously sequence exocentric view-selection to resolve severe occlusions. Finding 2: Premature Spatial Termination. Current models suffer from tendency to halt exploration prematurely. Human evaluators explicitly shift viewpoints in Model Avg. Acc (%) Model Avg. In contrast, the highest-performing model Gemini-3.5-flash averages only 2.5 steps. This indicates that MLLMs underestimate their own visual uncertainty, falsely concluding they have gathered sufficient geometric evidence when necessary details remain obscured. Finding 3: Breakdown on Spatial Geometry. During multi-turn view-exploration, models handle entity queries reasonably well, such as Gemini-3.5-flash scoring 68.2% on Object Existence, but fail on tasks requiring precise 3D geometric alignment. Accuracy plummets on Human-Object Interaction (31.9%) and View-Specific Depth Ordering (32.2%), highlighting bottleneck in tracking fine-grained coordinate transformations across dynamic perspective shifts. Finding 4: The High Inference Cost of Active Exploration. Active exploration imposes severe computational cost. Total inference latency for Gemini-3.5-flash surges to over 236% from 2.8 to 9.4 hours. This highlights that current MLLMs lack the memory-efficient caching required to sustainably process expanding multi-view contexts across continuous perspective exploration. Finding 5: Open-Source Models Lag in Visual SelfAwareness. Despite competitive baseline capabilities, open-source models struggle significantly in the Active setting compared to proprietary systems. While models like LLaVA-OneVision2-8B achieve moderate 58.9% accuracy in the Passive setting, their Active exploration rates are extraordinarily low, ranging from 0.0% to 5.8%. Consequently, their Active accuracies stagnate between 29% and 36%, revealing deficit in spatial proactivity and autonomous multi-turn planning. Finding 6: Limitations of Thinking Mechanism in Active Exploration. In the Passive setting, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking leverages extended inference to outperform the Instruct baseline (57.7% vs. 55.6%), demonstrating that internal reasoning aids static multiview fusion. However, this advantage vanishes in the Active setting, where the Thinking model underperforms Instruct (29.8% vs. 30.7%). Despite generating extensive chains-of-thought that inflate inference latency (> 20.0 vs. < 1.0 hours), it exhibits much lower active exploration rate (5.8% vs. 15.6%). Single View Evaluation To validate that our tasks cannot be solved through singleframe deduction alone, and to show the need for spatial exploration, we restrict models strictly to the initial occluded viewpoint, denying any spatial exploration, as detailed in Table 5. Finding 7: Model Scaling Cannot Overcome Physical Occlusion. When trapped in single ambiguous perspective, scaling model capacity yields no advantage. The compact GPT-5-mini (39.6%) marginally outperforms the larger models like GPT-5.2 (37.3%). Raw parameter counts cannot reconstruct obscured physical evidence. Without active view-exploration, models can only hallucinate or rely on linguistic priors, validating the difficulty of our benchmark and the necessity of active exploration. 4.4. Evaluation on Expanded View Selection To test if the strictly adjacent (1) view constraint limits performance, we evaluate an expanded setting allowing broader perspective shifts (1 or 2), as shown in Table 6. Finding 8: Static Accuracy. Despite the capacity to explore perspectives faster, overall accuracy remains virtually unchanged, with Gemini-2.5-flash shifting only marginally from 45.4% to 45.7%. This confirms that MLLM spatial reasoning failures stem from lack of visual self-awareness and failing to recognize uncertainty, rather than restricted querying mechanics. Finding 9: Marginal Efficiency Gains. While accuracy stagnates, the Average Reward slightly improves from 35.3 to 38.0. When models correctly elect to engage in viewexploration, the expanded options allow them to safely bypass redundant intermediate frames. Consequently, they can reach optimal unoccluded viewpoints more directly, accelerating the resolution of spatial ambiguity and thereby incurring fewer step penalties. Model Setting Avg. Acc (%) Avg. Steps Avg. Reward Active Rate (%) Gemini-3.1-lite Active Gemini-3.1-lite Passive Active GPT-5-mini Passive GPT-5-mini 38.0 40.3 41.4 41.9 1.5 - 1.4 - 31.5 - 34.0 - 24.8 - 29.4 - 4.5. Matched-View Evaluation To identify the failure, we evaluated Matched-View Passive control where the model receives the same views in the identical order as its corresponding Active trajectory. Finding 10: Active-Passive Gap Stems from Inadequate Exploration. As shown in Table 7, both settings achieve similar accuracy when provided with identical visual evidence. This confirms that the performance drop in the Active setting is primarily caused by insufficient evidence acquisition during exploration, rather than difficulties in processing the multi-turn format itself. 4.6. Long-Context Video Modeling Evaluation Recent long-context models could theoretically bypass sequential querying by treating spatial views as temporal stream. To test this, we formulated all Passive views as single video sequence. Finding 11: Video Modality Degrades Reasoning. However, it consistently degrades performance compared to standard multi-image inputs. Specifically, accuracy drops from 62.6% to 57.6% for Gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and from 64.6% to 63.7% for GPT-5-mini. This suggests that current video encoding is less effective at integrating discontinuous cross-camera views that lack natural temporal continuity. Explicitly framing discrete viewpoints as distinct images remains more effective strategy. 4.7. Direct Measurement of Visual Self-Awareness To directly measure visual self-awareness, we prompt models to report continuous confidence score (0100%) alongside their action decisions at each exploration step. Finding 12: Severe Overconfidence Drives Premature Stopping. As illustrated in Table 8, models exhibit severe overconfidence. Despite halting prematurely (averaging 1.4 steps) and achieving low overall accuracy, they report extremely high terminal confidence scores. This explicitly demonstrates that premature stopping is driven by false sense of certainty rather than arbitrary policy limits. 4.8. Error Analysis Our error analysis reveals distinct failure modes across different models. Closed-source models primarily fail 7 Figure 3. Impact of the action reward weight (r3) during GRPO fine-tuning on Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct. Increasing the action reward successfully incentivizes proactive behavior, evidenced by sharp rise in (b) average steps and (d) active exploration rate. However, this aggressive exploration exacerbates contextual interference, leading to steady decline in (a) active accuracy and (c) average reward. In contrast, the models passive accuracy remains highly stable across all reward configurations. Table 8. Analysis of exploration behavior and terminal confidence, from separate run with the confidence-elicitation prompt. Model names are abbreviated for brevity: Gemini-3.1-lite refers to Gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and GPT-5-mini refers to GPT-5-mini2025-08-07. Model Avg. Avg. Avg. Active Last 3rd Penult. Final Acc (%) Steps Reward Rate (%) Conf (%) Conf (%) Conf (%) Gemini-3.1-lite GPT-5-mini 37.3 41.4 1.4 1. 33.0 36.4 16.2 26.3 82.1 73.2 85.2 78.5 95.1 84.7 due to multi-view fusion bottlenecks and visual hallucinations across accumulated frames. Conversely, opensource models suffer from fundamental lack of proactivity. Reasoning-focused variants frequently fall into infinite internal deduction loops, exhausting token limits without executing concrete spatial actions. Meanwhile, standard instruction-tuned variants prematurely guess final answers despite severe occlusion. Given this pervasive deficit in autonomous exploration, critical question arises: can active exploration be elicited through reinforcement learning? 5. Can MLLMs Learn Active Exploration via Reinforcement Learning? Inspired by prior work [8, 27] and our Findings 5 and 6, we investigate whether MLLMs can acquire active exploration capabilities through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [43]. We synthesize 19.3K training samples from M3GYM and Ego-Exo4D using Gemini-3.5-flash, and fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on balanced 1:1 mixture of active and passive tasks. To reduce the computational complexity, we simplify the training as single-turn decision process: the model must either directly answer the question (passive) or select movement action to explore further (active). The GRPO reward function incorporates an accuracy reward (r1 = 1.0), format reward (r2 = 0.5), and an action reward (r3 [0.05, 1.4]). Results are shown in Figure 3. Detailed training data and hyperparameters are provided in the Appendix F. Finding 13: GRPO Boosts Active Exploration. Before tuning, the base Qwen2.5-VL-3B exhibits severe visual blindness. In the Active setting, it yields mere 0.2% active exploration rate and averages only 1.0 step per query, preferring to guess blindly rather than navigate away from occluded viewpoints. Post-tuning, the models willingness to explore surges dramatically; for instance, the model with 1.2 action reward weight achieves 72.8% active rate and averages 6.0 steps. This demonstrates that RL effectively incentivizes the behavioral logic of switching views when initial information is insufficient. Finding 14: Passive Multi-View Perception Remains Stable. When evaluated in the Passive setting, where static, complete multi-view evidence is provided simultaneously, both the Base and GRPO-tuned models maintain highly consistent accuracies (51.0%). This indicates that GRPO tuning does not degrade the models core multi-image feature fusion capabilities. It further validates the inherent ActivePassive performance gap, confirming that models struggle specifically with the dynamic planning and sequential reasoning required during active exploration. Finding 15: The Exploration-Accuracy Trade-off. Adjusting the action reward parameter reveals strict tradeoff in policy learning. While higher action rewards incentivize more exploration steps and improve the active rate, they concurrently induce an over-exploration penalty, leading to lower overall accuracy and degraded final rewards. 6. Conclusion We introduce SATE-Bench to evaluate visual selfawareness and active view-exploration in MLLMs. Our evaluations show that models underestimate visual uncertainty under occlusion, stopping prematurely with high confidence. While GRPO incentivizes active view-seeking, over-exploration and multi-view fusion bottlenecks lower accuracy. Ultimately, scaling passive perception cannot yield active spatial reasoning. 8 Acknowledgements. More Qualitative Examples We provide more qualitative examples in Figure 4. A.2. Details of Source Datasets SATE-Bench is constructed from ten high-quality, multiview, human-centered datasets designed to capture complex real-world spatial interaction scenarios, including severe occlusion, dynamic motion, and multi-person collaboration. These datasets complement each other in terms of scene structure, interaction types, and camera configurations, ensuring broad coverage of human-centered spatial reasoning scenarios. Core4D [35]. Core4D focuses on human-object-human collaborative interaction in unconstrained 3D environments. It captures scenes where multiple individuals simultaneously manipulate shared objects, often within tightly coupled spatial configurations. By explicitly capturing the intricate dynamics of object handover and joint manipulation, the severe mutual occlusion and overlapping interactions make Core4D particularly well-suited for evaluating cross-view reasoning, object association, and relative spatial localization capabilities in densely populated, shared workspaces. M3GYM [54]. M3GYM is large-scale multi-view motion dataset that captures high-intensity human activity It includes complex body movein gym environments. ments such as squats, weightlifting, and stretching exercises, which naturally induce severe self-occlusion and nonrigid pose deformations. The highly synchronized camera rings capture these rapid movements from varying elevations, making it ideal for evaluating fine-grained pose understanding, kinematic tracking, and action recognition under persistent occlusion. Harmony4D [25]. Harmony4D provides intensive multicamera recordings of human-to-human and human-toobject interactions in the wild. Its synchronized, highfidelity views enable fine-grained spatial alignment across cameras. By capturing close-proximity activities like wrestling and hugging, it is particularly useful for evaluating close-range physical contact reasoning, depth ordering, and multi-view geometric consistency. HOI-M3 [62]. HOI-M3 focuses on human-object interaction modeling in multi-view environments, emphasizing the fine-grained contact relationships between human body parts and manipulated objects. By incorporating detailed contextual environments, this dataset presents significant challenges due to uneven object visibility and ambiguous interactivity across different viewpoints, demanding robust 3D geometric projections from observing models. Ego-Exo4D [15]. Ego-Exo4D is massive-scale dataset containing paired egocentric (wearable) and other-centric (static exocentric) views of complex skilled human activities. By capturing synchronized activities such as cooking, sports, and mechanics, it enables reasoning across vastly different perspectives, effectively bridging the gap between first-person perception and third-person spatial reconstruction. EgoHumans [24]. EgoHumans captures wide variety of unscripted human activities in real-world environments from multiple simultaneous perspectives. It emphasizes natural movement and cluttered backgrounds across diverse indoor and outdoor settings. The introduction of varied lighting conditions and scale changes makes it highly suitable for evaluating model robustness under real-world occlusion and dynamic perspective shifts. MvMHAT [12]. MvMHAT is multi-view dataset designed to understand human movement and multi-person tracking under conditions of severe occlusion. It provides synchronized camera setups that capture subjects daily activities and interactions in 360-degree omnidirectional footage. The strategic placement of cameras challenges models to maintain spatial awareness of individuals as they transition through heavily occluded blind spots. Replay [44]. Replay offers multi-view recording capabilities with highly controllable camera positions, enabling the capture of both structured and unstructured social activities. Its high-fidelity recording of casual interactions provides rich geometric cues, making it widely used to evaluate temporal consistency, multi-view feature fusion, and robust cross-view correspondence in dynamic scenes. 4D-OR [37]. 4D-OR focuses on the clinical operating room environment, using dense multi-camera setup to capture the holistic surgical process. The clustering of medical staff around the surgical bed introduces extreme, sustained mutual occlusion caused by personnel and equipment. This makes it highly valuable for detailed spatial reasoning, depth estimation, and entity existence verification in critical medical settings. MM-OR [38]. MM-OR expands upon multimodal operating room data by providing richer step-by-step procedure annotations and enhanced multi-view synchronization capabilities. It serves as rigorous benchmark designed to aid Figure 4. Taxonomy and qualitative examples of SATE-Bench tasks. Our benchmark evaluates multi-view spatial reasoning across five core cognitive dimensions: Counting, Existence, Pose and Physical Interaction, Global Relative Proximity, and View-Specific Spatial Geometry. For each sub-task, we illustrate representative spatial query alongside subset of the available exocentric observations required to resolve the scenes geometric ambiguity. in understanding complex surgical workflows, tool tracking, and multi-person coordination under conditions of severely limited visual accessibility. A.3. Detailed Task Definitions To rigorously evaluate the capacity of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning and active exocentric view-exploration, we define ten distinct human-centric tasks distributed across five cognitive dimensions. Entity Counting (Human Counting & Object Counting). These tasks determine the total unique instances across complex scenes. In multi-camera environments, counting evaluates global spatial memory and cross-view re-identification. Models must actively resolve localized occlusions via continuous view-exploration, ensuring they track entities across perspective shifts without doublecounting. Entity Existence (Human Existence & Object Existence). These tasks verify the presence of specific visual targets that may be completely obscured in the initial view. This fundamentally tests fine-grained searching and visual self-awareness, assessing whether an MLLM can explicitly recognize its observational blind spots and execute an active 15 exploration policy to uncover geometric evidence, rather than relying on language priors to hallucinate an answer. Pose and Physical Interaction (Fine-grained Action and Pose & Human-Object Interaction). Comprehending dense human activity requires granular geometric alignment. These tasks analyze complex body kinematics and exact physical contact points. Models are challenged to resolve severe mutual occlusions and deceptive 2D projections by aggregating spatial evidence through active exocentric exploration. Global Relative Proximity (Relative Distance to Human & Relative Distance to Object). These queries require identifying the closest entity to designated 3D reference point. This dimension evaluates the models multiview depth estimation and cross-perspective distance reasoning, ensuring relative spatial relationships remain consistent even as the model shifts between discrete vantage points. View-Conditioned Spatial Geometry (View-Specific Depth Ordering & View-Specific Direction). These tasks demand dynamic coordinate frame alignment. Models must rank relative depth from specific target vantage point or predict 2D directional offsets (e.g., top-left) relative to designated anchor. This directly evaluates perspectivetaking and geometric projection, testing if the model can accurately map and transform spatial relationships outside of its current intrinsic observation point. A.4. Pre-processing We synchronize videos using official calibration data and extract 4 to 8 views per scene. These are manually sorted in clockwise order, ensuring uniform 360 distribution and full scene coverage. This normalizes the querying interface across diverse datasets, enabling standard left/right view exploration. A.5. Distractor Design Each 5-option QA pair contains one correct answer, three distractors, and one Abstention Option (e.g., target is invisible/unanswerable). To prevent models from exploiting linguistic priors without performing visual exploration, distractors are deterministically generated based on misleading view-specific artifacts and semantic/geometric proximity. A.6. Paired QA Analysis The Active and Passive settings share the same images, questions, and ground-truth answers, differing only in visual initialization. Specifically, while each Passive item provides comprehensive set of static views, its paired Active initializes the model with designated occluded viewpoint. Because every ActivePassive pair evaluates the exact same question, the performance gap in Table 4 provides direct comparison across settings. A.7. Data Leakage Analysis To rigorously prevent data leakage, all raw images in SATEBench are exclusively sourced from the official test splits of the human-centric multi-view datasets. For datasets lacking predefined splits, we manually construct held-out subset specifically for evaluation. Crucially, all question-answer pairs and spatial annotations are entirely novel, authored explicitly for this benchmark, and have never been publicly released or included in any prior training corpora. Similarly, the data utilized for GRPO fine-tuning is strictly isolated from the evaluation set. GRPO training samples are sourced exclusively from the official training splits of the original datasets. For datasets without explicit splits, the training data is sampled from disjoint subset that strictly excludes any scenes present in SATE-Bench. Furthermore, all QA pairs used for GRPO are newly synthesized, guaranteeing zero overlap with the benchmark annotations and eliminating the risk of test-set memorization. A.8. Human Baseline Evaluation To establish rigorous human performance upper bound, we recruit five independent postgraduate evaluators with backgrounds in Computer Science and Biomechanics. Participants complete the tasks without time restrictions via custom interactive Gradio interface, shown in Figure 5, which allows them to seamlessly execute discrete exocentric view-exploration queries. To mitigate interface familiarity bias, all evaluators undergo guided 20-question trial phase prior to the formal assessment. Crucially, to guarantee fair comparison, human participants are subjected to the identical step-wise exploration constraints as the evaluated MLLMs. They receive the exact same system prompts, task instructions, and environmental context, including the total camera count and circular layout, ensuring they navigate the 360-degree scenes under identical restricted visual conditions. In interaction questions, models also often report physical contact that does not exist (Case P1, Figure 8). C. Experiment Details C.1. Details of the baselines Baselines. To rigorously ground MLLM performance and disentangle the exploration policy from downstream spatial reasoning, we provide 9 baselines in total. By default, interaction histories are fully visible to models for all evaluations. The baselines include: Random Guess: Assumes uniform selection among given choices, yielding expected accuracies of 20% for 5-option formats and 50% for 2-option formats. Blind (Text-Only): Evaluates Gemini-2.5-flash exclusively on text prompts with all visual input completely withheld. This quantifies the extent of exploitable linguistic priors in the benchmark. Human Baseline: Averages the performance of five independent graduate evaluators (distinct from the annotation team). For the Active setting, these subjects interact with the identical step-wise 360 environment, establishing an upper bound for spatial reasoning and active exploration accuracy. Oracle-View: Evaluates performance when the model is directly provided with the single most informative viewpoint containing the unoccluded evidence. Oracle-Trajectory: Supplies the model with the optimal sequence of navigational steps to uncover the hidden evidence, isolating reasoning capabilities from pathplanning failures. Always Explore Left: Forces the model to follow predetermined, rigid sequence of viewpoints by continuously panning to the left. This provides smaller gains compared to active planning but isolates the benefit of simple, fixed exploration trajectory. Always Explore Right: Forces the model to continuously pan to the right. Together with the left-exploration baseline, this assesses whether simple fixed-order traversal is sufficient and checks for directional bias in the environment. Random-Walk Exploration: The agent traverses the environment using randomly selected navigational steps. improvement, This baseline typically offers minimal highlighting the necessity of deliberate planning over stochastic movement. Exhaustive-Search: Allows the model to sweep all possible viewpoints in the 360 environment before answering, testing its capacity for cross-view integration and memory retention over long contexts. Through these variations (the latter six evaluated using Gemini-3.1-flash-lite), we can pinpoint specific bottlenecks. For instance, comparing the active policy against Oracle, fixed-order, and random baselines reveals that premature stopping and ineffective viewpoint selection are major failure modes in the Active setting, though imperfect crossview integration remains contributing factor. Personally Identifying Information and Offensive Content In the curation of SATE-Bench, we implemented strict protocols to identify and mitigate the presence of Personally Identifying Information (PII) and offensive content. First, our benchmark is entirely derived from established, peerreviewed public datasets (e.g., M3GYM, Ego-Exo4D, 4DOR) that have already undergone their respective Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals and subject consent processes prior to their initial public release. During our multi-stage annotation and quality control pipeline, all 2,525 Question-Answer pairs and their corresponding multi-view frames are subjected to rigorous manual review by our annotation team. To protect individual identities, annotators are strictly prohibited from utilizing names, specific facial features, or any uniquely identifying metadata in the prompts, distractors, or ground-truth answers. Instead, all human subjects are referenced exclusively through generic physical descriptors, clothing attributes, or geometric spatial relationships, such as the person wearing red shirt and the individual closest to the surgical table. Furthermore, annotators are explicitly trained to flag and filter any frames or generated text containing offensive, harmful, or inappropriate content. Given that the source domains exclusively encompass structured environments, the inherent risk of offensive material is exceptionally low. Nevertheless, our independent cross-validation phase served as final safeguard, ensuring that all finalized benchmark materials are completely anonymized and adhere strictly to academic safety and ethical standards.
